interactions.summary: Students probe whether meritocracy still has redeeming fairness or efficiency, while Jiang insists that the lived outcome is hierarchical sorting, joylessness, and endless competition rather than genuine community.

speaker_notes.note: These are substantive student challenges and clarifications rather than throwaway comments; they articulate the strongest defenses of meritocracy that Jiang is rebutting.

claims.claim: A student says a pure meritocracy creates a culture of winners and losers and therefore must remain hierarchical by design.
Jiang contrasts meritocracy with a communal society in which people help one another instead of treating life as total competitive sorting.
A student defends meritocracy by saying it can give opportunity to people who did not win the birth lottery, but Jiang answers that this is the theory people have been taught.
A student links Jiang's meritocracy critique to earlier lecture arguments against pure logic: both promise ideal solutions while ignoring something deeper in human life.
Jiang says modern schooling trains children into endless competition, funnels them through more elite competition, and likely leaves them unhappy even when they succeed.
The class ends this packet with the open question of what system could replace meritocracy if its actual effect is hierarchical suffering.

signature_moments.moment: A pure meritocracy openly names the world as winners and losers.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It states the social psychology Jiang is trying to surface beneath arguments about fairness or efficiency.

signature_moments.moment: School becomes the pipeline that trains children to compete until adulthood without asking whether the process makes them happy.
signature_moments.source_phrase: kids go in and they compete against each other
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It makes Jiang's critique concrete and contemporary rather than leaving it at abstract moral philosophy.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's implied alternative to meritocracy: a social order organized around mutual help rather than winner-take-all hierarchy.

chronology_notes.note: This packet keeps the lecture in present-day application mode, deepening the critique of meritocracy rather than returning to close reading for the moment.

uncertainty_notes.note: The student's sentence is somewhat fragmented in ASR, but the comparison between meritocracy and earlier anti-logic themes is still interpretable.
